context: Orbit of x under a left group action, equivalent reached-set and action-equivalence-class formulations / reachable-set-orbit
editorial_note: Both ProofWiki orbit sections are directly accessible and explicitly give the reached-element description and the equivalence class of the action relation. These two formulations are equivalent for the SAME left group action because the group action relation is reflexive (identity), symmetric (inverse) and transitive (product). The action is required; the orbit is not a general topological orbit under flow and not necessarily finite. Do not confuse the size of an orbit with the orbit itself, or treat the set of all orbits as the orbit of one x. The equivalence class form involves a derived relation but does not require that a standalone abstract equivalence relation be the starting object. The group action can be on the empty set, but then there is no x whose orbit is defined. Right group actions, if later added, will require explicit orientation. Source sections: Definition 1 orbit as reached elements, Definition 2 equivalence class under action relation
text: Let G be a group acting on a set X on the left and x∈X. The orbit of x is G·x={g·x:g∈G}={y∈X:there exists g∈G with y=g·x}.

context: Point stabilizer (isotropy subgroup) for a specified left group action / fixing-elements-subset
editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly defines the stabilizer using elements fixing a selected x under G×X→X, and notes the synonyms isotropy group and G_x notation. It cites stabilizer-is-subgroup as a theorem; that property follows from the group action laws and is not silently treated as an independent defining axiom. The stabilizer is a subgroup of the ACTION GROUP G, not of the acted-on set X. It depends on the action as well as the point; the same group and point can yield different stabilizers for different actions. If X is empty then no x can be selected. This context is not a stabilizer in linear or geometric group actions unless that action is expressly given. No finiteness of G or transitivity assumed. Source sections: Theorem/Definition, Also denoted as, Also known as, Stabilizer is Subgroup cited as theorem
text: Let G act on X on the left and x∈X. The stabilizer of x in G is Stab_G(x)={g∈G:g·x=x}, the set of all elements of G fixing x under the given action.

context: Pushforward of a nonnegative measure through a measurable map of measurable spaces / preimage-evaluation-measure
editorial_note: ProofWiki defines pushforward of a measure μ on one measurable space along a Σ/Σ′-measurable map f by measuring inverse images of measurable target sets. The apparent arrow direction is important: source X to target Y but evaluation pulls sets backward before applying μ. Measurability ensures f^{-1}(B) lies in Σ, so the right side is defined; ordinary arbitrary set functions or nonmeasurable maps do not qualify. This is a new measure on the target measurable space, not image set f[X], and f_*μ is not literally composition with f, but composition μ∘f^{-1} acting on sets. The source shows extended-real codomain; the existing independent approved nonnegative measure meaning specifies [0,+∞], preserving positivity and infinity. It is distinct from pushforward of probability distributions only in generality; no normalization μ(X)=1 is assumed. Source sections: Definition, Also known as, Pushforward Measure is Measure cited
text: Let (X,Σ) and (Y,Τ) be measurable spaces, μ:Σ→[0,+∞] a measure, and f:X→Y a (Σ,Τ)-measurable map. The pushforward measure f_*μ on (Y,Τ) is defined for every B∈Τ by (f_*μ)(B)=μ(f⁻¹(B)).

context: Partition of a set into nonempty pairwise disjoint blocks, two equivalent characterizations / disjoint-cover-nonempty-blocks
editorial_note: ProofWiki supplies two equivalent definitions of an UNINDEXED set partition: pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets covering S, and exactly one block containing each point. Both permit an infinite set or infinite collection of blocks; no finite cardinality constraint is added. In particular, for S=∅ the empty collection is the unique partition, since nonempty-block and pointwise conditions are vacuous. The page additionally distinguishes an indexed partitioning (family indexed by an I) from the partition as the resulting set of distinct blocks; the source's indexed alternative is not merged as an identical data structure. These definitions do not assume an ordering on the blocks and do not give an equivalence relation directly, though partitions induce such a relation. A family permitting empty blocks is not a partition under the source's explicit convention. Source sections: Definition 1 pairwise disjoint, cover and nonempty blocks, Definition 2 each element belongs to exactly one nonempty block, Indexed partitioning distinguished
text: For a set S, a partition P is a collection of nonempty subsets B⊆S such that ⋃_{B∈P}B=S and B∩C=∅ whenever B,C∈P are distinct.
